notes:
I couldn't cover the whole chapter. **I found nothing for vv. 16 and 27–33.** The Enduring Word page cut off at v. 27, and the Precept Austin and Pulpit pages either cut off early or wouldn't load. I also found nothing from Lutheran, Orthodox, Bible Odyssey or NET Bible sources, apart from one NET note quoted on Precept Austin. The comparison between traditions only covers a few verses (13, 22–24).

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Jesus planned His arrival carefully: "Since the time was short before His crucifixion, Jesus left nothing to chance." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- Stein, quoted on Precept Austin, says that in Mark's layout this is Jesus' only entry into Jerusalem, while John records several visits. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-11-commentary
- A NET note quoted there says the Mount of Olives is really a ridge about 1.8 miles long, roughly 100 feet higher than Jerusalem. — same URL
- MacArthur (gty.org, quoted on Precept Austin) dates the entry to Monday, 10 Nisan. That was the day the Passover lamb was chosen; the crucifixion followed on the 14th. — same URL

**v. 2**
- Guzik says Jesus chose a young donkey on purpose. "In that day, to come riding a colt – as opposed to a mighty war-horse – was to come as a man of peace." This fulfils Zechariah 9:9. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- Guzik quotes Ironside: as the Creator, Jesus could ride an unbroken colt because all the lower creatures were subject to Him. — same URL
- Matthew Henry, on StudyLight, makes the same point: riding a colt never ridden before showed His rule over creation. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-11.html
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the village would most likely be Beth-phage. It notes that Mark mentions only the colt, while Matthew has the donkey and the colt. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/11-2.htm
- Ellicott says only Mark and Luke mention that no one had sat on it. — same URL

**v. 3**
- Coffman reads the Greek "back here" as the disciples bringing the colt back to Jesus, not Jesus returning it to its owner. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-11.html
- Precept Austin reads it the other way: Jesus only wanted to borrow the colt and would keep it no longer than needed. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-11-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary sees the stranger's agreement as recognising Jesus' authority as "the Lord". — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-11.html

**vv. 4–6**
- Guzik thinks Jesus had pre-arranged this with the colt owner. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- Peake's Commentary also describes it as if everything had been arranged beforehand. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-11.html

**v. 7**
- Akin, quoted on Precept Austin, says this is the one and only time Jesus rides an animal. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-11-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek could mean Jesus sat on the garments or on one of the two animals. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-11.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik says the cloaks served as both a saddle and a red carpet. Since clothing was costly, this was generous praise. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- Precept Austin cites 1 Maccabees 13:51 and says it was a conqueror's welcome they sought to give to Jesus. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-11-commentary

**vv. 9–10**
- The crowd's words come from Psalm 118, so their praise was Scriptural. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- Guzik notes that Jesus usually discouraged public acclaim as Messiah, but here He welcomed it. — same URL
- Bible Hub explains that "Hosanna" means "Save, please". — https://biblehub.com/mark/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary sees the procession as a picture of the resurrection, the ascension and the second coming. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-11.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik says Jesus was inspecting the temple, in line with Malachi 3:1–3. His public entry also took courage, since there was a price on His head (John 11:57). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- A commentary quoted on StudyLight says that from this day on, Jesus spent no night in the city except the last one. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-11.html

**vv. 12–14 (the fig tree)**
- Guzik: the tree was a picture of false advertising, having leaves but no figs. The tree was cursed for its pretense of leaves, not for its lack of fruit. This is Jesus' only destructive miracle. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- The Pulpit Commentary: the fig tree was cursed, not for being barren, but for being false. — https://biblehub.com/mark/11-13.htm
- Ellicott takes "not the season" in its natural sense: the early leaves suggested early figs, but the tree had none. — same URL
- Gill offers several options: the figs had not yet been picked, it was a bad fig year, or the tree was an unusual kind. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-13.html
- Bible.org: Jesus was looking for the edible buds, and their absence showed the tree would be fruitless that year. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-cursing-fig-tree
- Got Questions: fig fruit usually appears before the leaves. The curse symbolised judgement on Israel's empty religion. — https://www.gotquestions.org/curse-fig-tree.html
- Clarke: the curse did not come from resentment. It showed the disciples the judgement coming on the nation. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-13.html
- Matthew Henry: the curse reverses the first blessing, "Be fruitful". — same URL

**vv. 15–17 (the temple)**
- Guzik: the traders worked with the priests, overcharging pilgrims for approved animals and temple currency. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- The selling took place in the outer courts, the only place Gentiles could pray. That is why "for all nations" matters. — same URL
- Guzik says a "den of thieves" is where thieves gather and hide. — same URL
- R.C. Sproul (Reformed) links the two events. Mark places the temple scene between the cursing and the withering. Israel was "God's fig tree", cursed because its worship was hypocritical. — https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-fig-tree-and-temple

**vv. 18–19**
- Smith places the temple scene on the Monday after the entry. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-11.html

**vv. 20–21**
- Got Questions says the disciples were amazed, because a tree would normally take weeks to wither like this. — https://www.gotquestions.org/curse-fig-tree.html
- Desiring God says the withered tree was a sign of Israel's fruitlessness and echoes Jeremiah 8:13. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/he-cursed-the-barren-tree

**v. 22**
- Barnes says the Greek is literally "have the faith of God", meaning strong confidence in God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-23.html
- Benson says that wherever "faith" is joined to "of God", God is the subject or the object, so it is not just a figure of speech for "strong faith". — same URL
- Guzik cites Robertson, Wuest and the Expositor's commentary: God is the *object* of faith. The phrase cannot mean "have God's faith". — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/

**v. 23**
- Guzik: "mountain" was a common Jewish figure for an impossible problem. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- Matthew Henry thinks the mountain is the Mount of Olives. He applies the promise mainly to the apostles' miracle-working faith, and says it rests on a word from God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-23.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Jesus means spiritual obstacles, not physical ones. — same URL
- The Biblical Illustrator: "this mountain" was the temple mount, standing for the whole temple system that was about to pass away. — same URL

**v. 24**
- Gill limits the promise to requests that fit God's revealed will. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/mark/11-24.html
- Got Questions: this is not giving us a blank check to have whatever we want. — https://www.gotquestions.org/believe-that-you-have-received-it.html

**v. 25**
- Guzik: an unforgiving heart can hinder prayer just as unbelief does. Such a heart may be "bigger than any mountain". — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/

**v. 26**
- Bible Hub: the earliest and most geographically diverse Greek manuscripts of Mark omit the sentence. — https://biblehub.com/q/Why_omit_Mark_11_26_in_some_Bibles.htm
- It is missing from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others, but present in Alexandrinus, most medieval manuscripts and the Vulgate. — same URL
- It is probably a later addition copied from Matthew 6:15. — same URL

## Where Protestant traditions differ
- **v. 13, Baptist:** Spurgeon reads "the time of figs was not yet" as a picture of the elect who are not yet called but will be by irresistible grace. Israel had leaves early but no fruit. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-13.html
- **v. 13, Methodist:** Wesley's note reads the phrase as "not a good year for figs". — same URL
- **v. 22, Holiness:** Godbey (1896) separates faith *in* God (justification) from the "faith *of* God", a perfect faith with no doubt, which belongs to entire sanctification. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/mark/11-24.html
- **v. 22, Calvary Chapel:** Guzik rejects the "God's faith" reading (see v. 22 above). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- **v. 24, Reformed:** Sproul, quoted on Precept Austin, warns that a whole "name it and claim it" theology has been built almost entirely on this verse. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-11-commentary

## Other views
- **Catholic (vv. 13–23):** One catholic.com article says "not the season" is about theology, not gardening. The curse is a physical parable showing that the temple's time is ending. The withering came about through Jesus' faith in God. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/why-did-jesus-curse-the-fig-tree
- A second catholic.com article cites St. Josemaría Escrivá: the curse shows what Jesus thinks of making excuses. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/why-does-jesus-curse-the-fig-tree
- The Catholic Douay text of v. 22 reads "Have the faith of God." — https://biblehub.com/catholic/mark/11-22.htm
- **Critical view (v. 13):** Barclay (on StudyLight) raises the objection that cursing a tree for having no fruit out of season seems unreasonable and unjust. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/11-13.html
- **Word of Faith / prosperity (vv. 23–24):** Got Questions says Word of Faith teachers latch on to Mark 11:23 to claim a special power in their words, and calls that a twisting of the passage. — https://www.gotquestions.org/whoever-says-to-this-mountain.html
- Got Questions quotes Kenneth Hagin: "You can have whatever you say." — https://www.gotquestions.org/decree-and-declare.html
- Monergism: these verses are not permission to create reality through confident speech. — https://www.monergism.com/word-faith-movement
- Guzik quotes Wiersbe calling the idea that God must answer if you "really believe" mere "faith in faith, or faith in feelings." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
- One gentler view: a Bible Hub article says positive confession can express reliance on God, but must stay under His sovereign will. — https://biblehub.com/q/define_positive_confession..htm
